title: How to set the DOCUMENT_ROOT and site root in my local PHP dev setup?

content: # Resolving Document Root Discrepancies in Local PHP Development When working on a client's environment, it is common to encounter a mismatch between the URL path used in browser requests and the physical directory structure on your local machine. This issue often manifests when `$_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT']` does not align with the expected location of assets, causing relative paths like `` to fail locally even though they work perfectly on production. The core of this problem lies in how PHP determines the document root. On a live server, the web server configuration (such as Apache's `VirtualHost` or Nginx's `server_root`) explicitly defines the directory that corresponds to the site's root URL. When you access `http://example.com/`, the server serves files starting from `/var/www/example.com`. Consequently, a request for `/images/shopping.gif` translates internally to `/var/www/example.com/images/shopping.gif`. In a local development setup using MAMP or similar tools, the situation is less rigid. By default, MAMP often binds `http://localhost/` to the root of the MAMP installation directory (e.g., `/Applications/MAMP/www`). If your project resides at `http://localhost:8888/_CLIENTS/clientsite/www/`, the web server may still interpret the leading slash in your image tags as relative to the default MAMP root, not the specific client folder. To resolve this without modifying the production code or risking the live site, you must ensure that your local environment mimics the production document root logic. The most direct approach is to configure your virtual host settings to point to the correct directory. If you are using Apache within MAMP, locate the `httpd-vhosts.conf` file (usually found in `/Applications/MAMP/etc/`). You need to add or modify a `` block that matches your specific port and domain. For instance: ```apache ServerName localhost DocumentRoot "/path/to/_CLIENTS/clientsite/www" Options +Indexes FollowSymLinks MultiViews AllowOverride All Order allow,deny Allow from all ``` By setting `DocumentRoot` to the absolute path of your client's folder (e.g., `/path/to/_CLIENTS/clientsite/www`), Apache will treat that directory as the root for requests made on port 8888. Now, when PHP executes `$_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT']`, it will return the path to `_CLIENTS/clientsite/www`, and the relative path `/images/shopping.gif` will resolve correctly to the asset file within that folder. If you prefer a virtual host entry that maps to a subdirectory rather than the root directory itself, ensure your `ServerName` or `ServerAlias` matches the requested URL exactly. However, relying on subdirectory mapping in local setups can sometimes introduce complexity regarding rewrite rules and `.htaccess` directives. It is generally safer to configure the virtual host to serve the project from its own dedicated directory. Another consideration involves how you access the site. If your production environment uses a domain name like `clientsite.com`, but your local setup relies on a subdirectory structure, you might need to adjust your browser's address bar or your MAMP configuration to ensure the URL scheme matches expectations. While PHP does not inherently enforce the document root based solely on the URL path without server-side configuration, modern web servers handle this via rewrite rules if necessary. For environments where Apache configuration is cumbersome, MAMP includes a feature in its Preferences panel under "Apache" or "PHP" to manage multiple domains and ports. You can create a new site entry pointing specifically to your `_CLIENTS/clientsite/www` directory. This creates an isolated virtual host that behaves exactly like the production server regarding `$_SERVER` variables. It is crucial to remember that changes to Apache configurations require restarting the MAMP servers for them to take effect. Failure to do so will result in the web server continuing to serve from the default document root, perpetuating the broken image links. Always verify your setup by checking the value of `$_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT']` directly in a PHP file located in your project's root directory. If the output matches your expected path, your asset loading issues should be resolved. For developers who frequently switch between local and production environments, maintaining consistent server configurations is key to avoiding these discrepancies. Tools that manage virtual hosts effectively allow you to replicate the production document root locally without touching the live site files.
